name: Executive order of January 18, 1881 setting apart the Spokane Reservation
promises: This was an executive order, not a treaty. The President set apart a reserve for the occupancy of the Spokane, bounded by Chamokane Creek, the Spokane River, the Columbia River and the 48th parallel (Royce area 625).
Royce notes this was land that had formed part of the first Colville reservation of April 9, 1872, relinquished on July 2, 1872.

breaches.what: Congress granted to the United States, for the Columbia Basin Project and Grand Coulee Dam, all the right, title and interest of the Spokane and Colville tribes in tribal and allotted land within their reservations as the Secretary of the Interior designated, with compensation set by the Secretary; no tribal consent is stated.

source.title: 16 U.S. Code 835d, Acquisition of Indian lands for Grand Coulee Dam (Act of June 29, 1940)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

breaches.what: Congress found that under the 1940 Act the Secretary paid the Spokane Tribe $4,700, that Spokane tribal acreage was taken by the United States for the dam, and that the tribe suffered significant harm from the dam's construction and operation, and provided annual payments as fair and equitable compensation.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Spokane Tribe of Indians of the Spokane Reservation Equitable Compensation Act, Public Law 116-100, section 2, 133 Stat. 3256

source.title: Public Law 116-100, Spokane Tribe of Indians of the Spokane Reservation Equitable Compensation Act (December 20, 2019)

breaches.quote: the Spokane Tribe has suffered significant harm from the construction and operation of Grand Coulee Dam

landTaken: Spokane reservation land designated for the Grand Coulee Dam and its reservoir under the 1940 Act. Congress found the Spokane acreage taken equalled approximately 39 percent of the Colville tribal acreage taken; no Spokane acreage figure was found in a source opened.
compensation: $4,700 paid under the 1940 Act. The 2019 Act provides annual payments from the Bonneville Power Administration from March 1, 2022: 25 percent of the Colville settlement's computed annual payment through 2029 and 32 percent from 2030.
today: Congress found that the Spokane Tribe had settled its Indian Claims Commission land claims in 1967 and so, unlike the Colville Tribes, had no claim to amend for Grand Coulee. That 1967 compromise (Dockets 331 and 331-A, $6,700,000) concerned Spokane aboriginal title, which the Commission found the tribe held until July 13, 1892; it is not a finding about the reservation. Whether the 2019 payments have been made was not checked.

plain.promised: Not a treaty: a presidential order setting apart the Spokane Reservation between Chamokane Creek, the Spokane and Columbia rivers and the 48th parallel for the Spokane people to live on.
plain.happened: A 1940 Act of Congress took Spokane reservation land for the Grand Coulee Dam and paid $4,700. In 2019 Congress found Spokane land was taken for the dam and the tribe suffered significant harm.
plain.today: The 2019 Act set annual payments to the Spokane Tribe from 2022 as compensation for the dam's use of its land. Whether they have been paid was not checked.

openQuestions: The 1940 Act text was read on the Cornell US Code page (16 U.S.C. 835d), not in the Statutes at Large scan; sections 835e to 835h were not read for any consent or valuation terms.
A Bonneville Power Administration statement reported in search results gives about 2,500 acres of Spokane reservation land taken; that document was not opened, so no acreage is recorded.
Later reductions of the Spokane Reservation, if any, were not researched.
The Spokane Tribe's own account of Grand Coulee was not located on its website in this pass.
